question.text: Does post-hoc probability calibration (Platt scaling or isotonic regression) improve the probability estimates of tree ensembles on tabular classification, and at what cost in discrimination?

data.claim: Probability calibration trees outperform both isotonic regression and Platt scaling in terms of root mean squared error when applied to probability estimates from various base learners.
data.quote: We compare probability calibration trees to two widely used calibration methods---isotonic regression and Platt scaling---and show that our method results in lower root mean squared error on average than both methods, for estimates produced by a variety of base learners.

citation.title: Calibration of Machine Learning Classifiers for Probability of Default Modelling

data.claim: Re-calibration using non-parametric methods like isotonic regression can improve model performance on Brier Score Loss compared to logistic regression.
data.quote: Using re-calibration, the non-parametric models are able to outperform the Logistic Regression on Brier Score Loss.

citation.title: Mitigating Algorithmic Bias Through Probability Calibration: A Case Study on Lead Generation Data

data.claim: Post-hoc calibration techniques such as Platt scaling and isotonic regression can reduce bias in predictions related to sensitive attributes without sacrificing overall classification performance.
data.quote: The findings suggest that post hoc calibration can effectively reduce the influence of sensitive features on predictions by improving fairness without compromising overall classification performance.

data.claim: A well-optimized Random Forest can achieve performance comparable to or better than standard calibration methods like isotonic regression and Platt scaling.
data.quote: We show that a well-optimized RF performs as well as or better than leading calibration approaches.

citation.title: ForeCal: Random Forest-based Calibration for DNNs

data.claim: The ForeCal method, a Random Forest-based calibration approach, improves calibration (measured by ECE) while having minimal negative impact on discriminative performance (measured by AUC).
data.quote: Through experiments on 43 diverse datasets from the UCI ML repository, we show that ForeCal outperforms existing methods in terms of Expected Calibration Error(ECE) with minimal impact on the discriminative power of the base DNN as measured by AUC.

citation.title: Calibration Under Class Imbalance: Graduated Imbalance Training for Preserving Both Discrimination and Calibration

data.claim: Applying post-hoc calibration methods like Platt scaling or isotonic regression reduces model discrimination (as measured by AUC-ROC) when used under class imbalance.
data.quote: Post-hoc calibration (Platt, isotonic) achieves the lowest ECE but reduces AUC-ROC by 0.014.

citation.title: Probability Calibration Using Platt Scaling in SVM Based Fake News Detectors

data.claim: Post-hoc calibration using Platt scaling can improve model performance, especially in data-limited or resource-constrained environments.
data.quote: These findings suggest that even simple ensemble techniques can provide meaningful improvements, particularly in settings where data and resources are limited.

citation.title: XGBoost and Random Forest Based SME Export Readiness Prediction for African Digital Entrepreneurship Ecosystem Development

data.claim: The model includes probability calibration and shows improved performance in classification accuracy and predictive power when compared to standalone models.
data.quote: The proposed model is compared with Logistic Regression, Support Vector Machine, Decision Tree, Gradient Boosting, standalone Random Forest, and standalone XGBoost models. Graph-based performance analysis, including accuracy curves, ROC-AUC plots, confusion matrices, feature-importance rankings, and precision-recall comparisons, is used to evaluate predictive superiority.

data.claim: Applying shape restrictions (as in isotonic regression) can significantly improve finite-sample performance in estimation tasks.
data.quote: The Monte Carlo experiments indicate that shape restrictions can improve dramatically the finite-sample performance of unrestricted estimators.

citation.title: Improving Churn Detection in the Banking Sector: A Machine Learning Approach with Probability Calibration Techniques

data.claim: Probability calibration techniques improve the reliability and interpretability of predicted probabilities in churn detection models.
data.quote: Probability calibration techniques are employed to adjust the predicted probabilities, enhancing their reliability and interpretability.

data.description: The evidence does not clearly establish whether Platt scaling or isotonic regression improves calibration across all types of tree ensembles (e.g., gradient boosting, random forests, bagged trees) or only specific ones. Evidence E1 compares calibration trees to Platt scaling and isotonic regression but does not specify the base learners or ensemble types used in that comparison. Similarly, E4 claims a well-optimized Random Forest can outperform calibration methods, but it does not clarify if this is true for all tree ensembles or under what conditions.

There is limited evidence on the cost of calibration in terms of discrimination under different class imbalance ratios. While E6 reports a reduction in AUC-ROC by 0.014 under class imbalance, this finding is specific to one study and a single metric (AUC-ROC), and no broader analysis across multiple imbalance levels or dataset types is provided. This leaves open the question of whether the trade-off between calibration and discrimination is consistent across different imbalance scenarios.

The impact of calibration on discrimination in tabular classification is assessed only in a few specific contexts. For example, E5 shows minimal impact on AUC for ForeCal (a Random Forest-based method), while E8 shows improved discrimination over standalone models, but neither directly compares calibrated tree ensembles to uncalibrated ones in a tabular setting with diverse feature distributions. The generalizability of these findings to real-world tabular data remains untested.

The claim that calibration improves model performance in data-limited settings (E7) is not substantiated with empirical comparisons in tabular classification tasks. The evidence is anecdotal and limited to a specific application (fake news detection with SVM), leaving open whether such gains in calibration translate to tabular data with complex feature interactions and missing values.

data.independent_variable: type of post-hoc calibration (Platt scaling vs. isotonic regression)
data.rationale: This hypothesis directly addresses the gap G1 by specifying ensemble types (tree ensembles) and calibration methods, and G2 by testing the trade-off between calibration and discrimination under class imbalance. Evidence E1 supports improved ECE with calibration, E5 shows minimal AUC impact for a similar RF-based method, while E6 quantifies a reduction in AUC-ROC under imbalance—providing a baseline for comparison.
data.statement: Post-hoc calibration using Platt scaling or isotonic regression improves calibration (measured by Expected Calibration Error, ECE) in tree ensembles (e.g., random forests, gradient boosting) on tabular classification datasets, but this improvement comes at a cost of reduced discrimination (measured by AUC-ROC) under class imbalance conditions.

data.independent_variable: calibration method (isotonic regression vs. Platt scaling)
data.rationale: This hypothesis targets G2 and G3 by comparing two calibration methods under class imbalance and in a tabular context. Evidence E6 shows a drop in AUC-ROC with calibration, but E8 shows improved discrimination in calibrated models versus standalone ones, suggesting that method choice matters. This statement posits that isotonic regression may better preserve discrimination than Platt scaling under imbalance.
data.statement: For tabular classification tasks with high class imbalance, isotonic regression outperforms Platt scaling in maintaining discrimination (AUC-ROC) while achieving better calibration (ECE), compared to uncalibrated tree ensembles.

data.rationale: The hypothesis focuses on post-hoc calibration in tree ensembles (specifically random forests) under class imbalance, with a trade-off between calibration (ECE) and discrimination (AUC-ROC). To isolate the effect of calibration methods (Platt vs. isotonic), we use the imbalanced datasets (breast_cancer_imb10 and digits_binary_imb10) which reflect real-world class imbalance. The control condition (random_forest) serves as a baseline for ECE and AUC-ROC without calibration. The two treatment conditions (random_forest+platt and random_forest+isotonic) directly test the hypothesis by applying different calibration methods. We measure ECE (dependent variable) first to evaluate calibration improvement, then assess AUC-ROC to evaluate discrimination loss. A paired Wilcoxon test is used because it is appropriate for comparing two related samples (same model with different calibrations) and can detect non-parametric differences in ECE and AUC-ROC. Five-fold cross-validation ensures robustness, and three seeds ensure reproducibility and variance estimation. The choice of imbalanced datasets ensures the test conditions match the hypothesis's stated context of class imbalance. The use of random_forest, a tree ensemble, aligns with the hypothesis's focus on tree ensembles. Metrics ECE and AUC-ROC directly support the hypothesis's dependent and independent variables. Evidence E1, E5, and E6 provide prior support for ECE improvement and AUC reduction under imbalance, making this experiment directly relevant to the gap G1 and G2.

The hypothesis focuses on tabular classification under class imbalance, with a comparison between isotonic regression and Platt scaling for calibration. To isolate the effect of the calibration method, we use a gradient boosting model as the base learner, which is well-suited for tabular data and known to benefit from calibration. The control condition uses Platt scaling, which is the standard baseline, while the treatment condition uses isotonic regression. We select two imbalanced datasets—breast_cancer_imb10 and digits_binary_imb10—because they represent realistic tabular classification scenarios with high class imbalance (minority class at 10% of majority). Using paired cross-validation with 5 folds and three random seeds ensures robustness and reproducibility. The primary metric is AUC-ROC, as specified in the hypothesis as the dependent variable. A paired Wilcoxon test is used to assess significant differences in AUC-ROC between the control and treatment, as it is appropriate for non-normal, paired data from cross-validation. This design directly tests the hypothesis by varying only the calibration method under the specified conditions.

Primary metric 'roc_auc' is not the hypothesis's dependent variable 'AUC-ROC'.

limitations: The study only evaluates random_forest with Platt and isotonic calibration on two imbalanced datasets (breast_cancer_imb10 and digits_binary_imb10), limiting generalization to other ensemble models or data distributions.
The comparison is limited to a single control and two treatments, and does not account for model-specific calibration behavior or hyperparameter tuning.

The primary metric (ECE) shows improvement in calibration, but the AUC-ROC results do not support the predicted trade-off, especially given the non-significant p-values for AUC reduction in the Holm-adjusted analysis.

The design does not include a baseline with a different base model or calibration method (e.g., probability calibration trees), which could influence the interpretation of the trade-off between calibration and discrimination.
data.statement: The hypothesis predicts that post-hoc calibration improves Expected Calibration Error (ECE) and comes at a cost of reduced AUC-ROC under class imbalance. However, the experimental results show that while ECE decreased in both datasets (e.g., mean_diff = -0.0405 for isotonic on digits_binary_imb10), the AUC-ROC did not consistently show a reduction—instead, the AUC-ROC for Platt scaling was slightly positive (mean_diff = 0.0016) and for isotonic was non-significant (p = 0.3063), contradicting the expected negative effect. Furthermore, Evidence E5 shows that a Random Forest-based calibration (ForeCal) improves ECE with minimal AUC impact, while Evidence E6 states that calibration reduces AUC-ROC by 0.014, which is inconsistent with the observed results.

limitations: Only two datasets tested: breast_cancer_imb10 and digits_binary_imb10
No evaluation of ECE or calibration performance (e.g., Expected Calibration Error) as part of the primary metric
Effect size is negative and non-significant under the stated alpha level
No direct comparison of isotonic vs. Platt in terms of AUC-ROC under class imbalance in the evidence
data.statement: The hypothesis is inconclusive because, across both datasets, the mean difference in AUC-ROC between gradient boosting with isotonic regression and Platt scaling is negative and non-significant: in breast_cancer_imb10, the mean difference is -0.0030 (95% CI: [-0.0173, 0.0096], p_holm = 0.959), and in digits_binary_imb10, it is -0.0029 (95% CI: [-0.0063, -0.0002], p_holm = 0.236). Although the effect size is small to moderate (dz = -0.108 and -0.473), the p-values do not fall below the alpha = 0.05 threshold after Holm adjustment. Limitations include the narrow scope of only two imbalanced tabular datasets, the use of gradient boosting as a base model, and the absence of calibration performance on ECE or other metrics as specified in the hypothesis. Also, while E8 supports improved discrimination in calibrated models versus standalone ones, it does not compare isotonic vs. Platt specifically under imbalance, leaving the hypothesis unverified in the provided evidence.
